# dsh-mcp-relay
English | 简体中文

Expose a running DeepSeek Harness (DSH) instance over the
Model Context Protocol, so an external age

nt — Codex, or any MCP client —
can drive that instance's own sessions.
A DSH session behaves like a subagent from the caller's point of view: it keeps its own context acro

ss calls,
works in the workspace you name, and returns a final answer. The relay also lets the calle

r answer the
questions that DSH agent asks, so a delegated task never deadlocks waiting for a human
tions that DSH agent asks, so a delegated task never deadlocks waiting for a human who is not there.
## Why
Driving a DSH instance through its web GUI from another agent costs a screenshot or DOM round trip p

er step.
This relay replaces that with a small structured API: one tool call in, one result out.
## Architecture
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Two halves, and the split matters:
- **`lib/index.js`** is a DSH host plugin. It runs in the same process as the Web GUI, so it can rea

d and
write the sessions that instance already has. It registers an HTTP route and does the DSH work

.
- **`bin/dsh-mcp-relay.mjs`** is a standalone MCP server that speaks stdio to your agent and HTTP

to the plugin.
It exists because DSH's own process owns stdout, so the plugin cannot serve stdio its

he plugin.
It exists because DSH's own process owns stdout, so the plugin cannot serve stdio itself.
Waiting and polling happen in the MCP server, where they cost nothing, and `dsh_delegate` blocks by

default:
your model spends **one** tool call per delegated turn and receives the finished result.
The tool surface is deliberately small. The handshake instructions and every tool schema are re-sent

with
each model request, so each of them is a recurring cost rather than a one-off. Keep the defaul

t `wait: true`
and let it block — an async delegation that then gets short-polled costs one full req
and let it block — an async delegation that then gets short-polled costs one full request per poll.
## What a Codex caller pays
An MCP client re-sends the handshake instructions and every tool schema with each model request, so

that
text is a recurring cost rather than a one-off. Since 0.6.1 the surface is sized for that:
- the instructions are ~2.1k characters instead of ~4.3k, and the seven tool schemas ~4.2k instead o

te` blocks by default, so one delegated turn costs one model request, and polling is left to
callers
that genuinely have other work to do in parallel.
Waiting has a purpose rule, not just an interval rule: these tools exist to deliver a result, not pr

ogress
updates. Let `dsh_delegate` block unless you have independent work that can start now; finish

that work,
then collect the result with `dsh_poll` and a long `timeoutMs`. A `timeout` ends the wai

t — it is not a
failure, and "still running" is not a reason to keep querying and narrating progress

— it is not a
failure, and "still running" is not a reason to keep querying and narrating progress.

One limit sits outside this plugin: an MCP client may cap a single tool call (Codex exposes
`tool_ti

meout_sec`). A cap shorter than the relay's own wait turns one blocking delegation into repeated
rou
nd trips, and no prompt can undo that — give it at least `DSH_RELAY_TIMEOUT_MS`. For Codex:

The effect is measurable rather than asserted:

`DSH_RELAY_SURFACE=full` serves the older, larger surface, so the same task can be run against both

and
compared. The saving per request is small next to a long conversation's history; what matters is

that it is
paid on *every* request rather than once.
## Requirements

- DSH with a Web profile (`dsh web` or the desktop app).
- Node.js 18 or newer on the same machine a

s DSH.
- An MCP client that can spawn a stdio server.

ose

## Security
The relay is a control surface: whoever can reach it can send instructions to, and read the history

of, every
session in that DSH instance.
- It **serves loopback callers only** and answers `403` to anything else. This matters because the s

hipped Web
profile binds `0.0.0.0`.
- Set `DSH_RELAY_TOKEN` on both sides to additionally require an

`x-dsh-relay-token` header.
- The route is registered directly on DSH's HTTP server, so it is **not

** covered by the `/api` trusted-host
fence. Its own checks above are the only gate.
## Limitations

- The MCP server and DSH must run on the same machine, because the relay is loopback-only.
- One del

egated turn is bounded by `DSH_RELAY_TIMEOUT_MS`; there is no streaming of partial output.
- `cancel

` stops the active turn only — messages already queued in DSH keep running.
- The plugin reads a ses

sion's tail through `sessionController.page`, so a very large session reports its
recent history rat

`sessionController.page`, so a very large session reports its
recent history rather than all of it.
